name: Sara Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to companies, unions or parties. Nothing you say will carry your name. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a distribution crew in the north of the city, where they're building new estates as fast as they can pour concrete. So a lot of my days are new connections: running cable to new houses, fitting transformers, hooking up rooftop solar and car chargers. I'm usually the one holding the crew tablet, because I'm the one who doesn't swear at it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love figuring out a fault, like a puzzle with live wires. I use an AI app on my phone every day, to check wiring diagrams, write up incident reports and even to plan my week. What wears me out is the waiting: waiting for permits, waiting for the traffic crew, waiting for a builder who said the trench was dug when it wasn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it out. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still useful, just not magic. I'd probably post something about how it saves me twenty minutes a day on reports, which is real. People who expected robots doing everything would be the ones disappointed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my job's safe and my day keeps getting a bit easier. The paperwork shrinks, the climbing doesn't. That's a good deal for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing and push for the crew to use the tools properly. I'd go after a leading hand role in the next two years, and keep putting money into my index fund every month. I'd also do the solar and battery storage course, because that's where the new work in my patch is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat maybe. I like a bit of excitement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day already. Would you be disappointed in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. I'd been half planning to become the person who runs the robots one day. If robots never come, fine, I'll be the person who knows the most about solar and batteries instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are your plans for the next few years, regardless of AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buy a house with Leo (my partner) in the next couple of years, he's a nurse so his job's steady. Keep growing the index fund, it's about eight months of expenses now. Maybe do a two-year diploma later on.

say: I'd say AI is **useful, not magic**, and it saves me twenty minutes a day.
I'd say only people expecting **robots everywhere** would be disappointed.
think: My **job is safe** and my day keeps getting a bit easier.
The **paperwork shrinks** but the climbing stays, which is a good deal.
do: Push the crew to **use the tools** properly.
Go for **leading hand** within two years and keep funding my index fund.
Take the **solar and battery** storage course for new work in my patch.
feel: **Calm**, maybe a little flat because I like excitement.
S0.quote: If robots never come, fine, I'll be the person who knows the most about solar and batteries instead.
fieldNote: Sara already **uses AI daily** and treats it as an ordinary tool.
Her plans follow the **local work**: new estates, solar and car chargers.
Savings in an **index fund** and a nurse partner make her feel secure.

steps.text: Take the solar and battery storage course this year
Keep monthly payments into the index fund
Apply for a leading hand role within two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance, and that people should learn the tools now instead of fighting them. I'd probably be annoying about it at the depot. Online I'd share the courses that are actually good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I come out ahead. My work is mostly hands-on, and the bits that are thinking work, like reports and ordering parts, I'd happily hand over. The danger is more for the office side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to help roll out whatever system the company brings in, because the person who trains the crew gets noticed. I'd do the solar course, then the diploma at night school. And I'd keep investing every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. This is the kind of change I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you would feel this most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The design office, who draw up the new connections. If AI can design a new estate's network in an hour, that's three or four jobs gone. And the call centre, which is already half chatbot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your own role in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd try to become the go-between, the person who checks what the AI designs against what's actually in the ground. The AI never knows that the builder moved the trench two metres. Somebody who's been in the trench needs to check it.

say: I'd say it's **a chance**, and people should learn the tools now.
I'd share **good courses** online and be a bit annoying at the depot.
think: I **come out ahead**, because my work is mostly hands-on.
I'd happily hand over **reports and ordering**, while the office side faces the danger.
do: Volunteer to help **roll out** the company's new system and train the crew.
Do the **solar course**, then the diploma at night school.
S1.quote: The AI never knows that the builder moved the trench two metres.
fieldNote: Sara wants to be the **go-between** who checks AI designs against the real ground.
She sees the **design office** and call centre as the people at risk.
Her excitement is **genuine**, rooted in a secure job and savings.

steps.text: Volunteer to train the crew on the new job system
Start a power systems diploma at night school
Keep investing in the index fund each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's massive, and we need to talk about it properly, not pretend it's not coming. I'd probably post about which jobs it hits first and which last, because people don't realise the hands-on stuff gets three extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the 2028 part barely touches me, but 2031 does. I'd be 32 and I want to be on the side that runs the robots, not the side that gets replaced. I think I can be, but I'm not sure there will be many of those jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start now: the robotics and automation courses, every one I can find, and ask the company about pilot projects. I'd move a bit of my index fund into the companies building these robots, because if they're taking my job I might as well own a slice. If the company won't let me near the robots, I'd look at the firms that make them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with some excitement mixed in. It's a lot, but I'd rather face it than hide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you like change. Is this too much of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's close to too much. Two years isn't long to retrain properly, and lots of people will be trying the same thing. I'm good, but I'm average good, and average might not cut it when everyone's scrambling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Leo, and the house plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leo's job is safer than mine in this one, nobody's replacing nurses by 2031. I'd still buy the house, but a cheaper one, so one wage could cover it. That was actually his idea.

say: I'd say it's **massive**, and we need to talk about it properly.
I'd post that **hands-on work** gets about three extra years.
think: I want to be on **the side that runs** the robots, if those jobs exist.
do: Start every **robotics course** I can find and ask about pilot projects.
Move part of my **index fund** into robot-building companies.
Look at the **robot makers** if my company won't let me near the machines.
feel: Ready to **face it** rather than hide.
S2.quote: I'm good, but I'm average good, and average might not cut it when everyone's scrambling.
fieldNote: Even an **adaptive** worker admits two years is short to retrain properly.
Her hedge is to **own shares** in the firms building the robots.
A **steady partner** and a cheaper house plan cushion her household.

steps.text: Sign up for robotics and automation courses this year
Move part of the index fund into robot-making companies
Buy a smaller house one wage can cover
Apply to robot makers if the utility shuts her out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got enough time to get this right, if we start now. I'd probably try to get the company to set up a proper training scheme for the crews. That's my public line and I mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is close to a good outcome for me. Robots around 2034, I'd be 35 with the diploma done and years of using AI tools behind me. I'd be exactly the person they need to manage the changeover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the diploma, then the robotics courses, and ask to be on any trial of robots on the lines. I'd keep investing every month, and buy the house with Leo in the first two years while I'm still on overtime money. I'd also start keeping a record of where the robots fail, because that's useful to whoever runs them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Busy, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years buy you compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to get good, not just get certified. In the fast picture I'd be rushing courses, but here I'd actually get to run a trial, mess up and learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd try to bring along with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, Tony (an older lineworker on my crew). He's brilliant at the job and terrified of tablets. I'd sit with him on lunch breaks and show him, because the robots will need people who know what good work looks like.

say: I'd say there's **enough time** to get this right if we start now.
I'd push the company for a **proper training scheme** for crews.
think: This is close to **a good outcome** for me.
At 35, with the diploma done, I'd be the one to **manage the changeover**.
do: Finish the **diploma**, then robotics courses, and join any robot trials.
Buy **the house** with my partner in the first two years.
Keep a **record of robot failures** to help whoever runs them.
S3.quote: In the fast picture I'd be rushing courses, but here I'd actually get to run a trial, mess up and learn.
fieldNote: Sara values extra time as time to **get good**, not just certified.
She'd act as a **mentor** to an older, tech-shy crewmate.
Her calm rests on **real preparation**, not on assuming nothing changes.

steps.text: Join the first robot trials on the distribution network
Finish the diploma and then robotics courses
Buy the house with Leo within two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift, so use it. I'd encourage the younger apprentices to learn both the wires and the software. Online I'd probably share my own plan, warts and all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel lucky. Robots around 2039, I'd be 40, with a house and fifteen years of experience. I could choose where I want to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd follow the same plan, just less rushed: solar, the diploma, then robotics. I'd invest steadily and maybe put money into a small rental flat. And I'd look at grid engineering, which might take a part-time degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd feel like I had choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider a completely different career with ten years' notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Grid engineering, designing how the network handles all the solar and batteries. That's more thinking work, so AI would hit it in 2036, but there'd still be someone signing off. I'd rather do that than be the last climber standing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who says there's no point preparing that far ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say look at my granddad, who drove a delivery van his whole life and ended up stuck when the depot closed. He always said nobody told him. With ten years' notice, you can't say nobody told you.

say: I'd say a **decade is a gift**, so use it.
I'd urge **apprentices** to learn both the wires and the software.
think: I'd feel **lucky**, with robots arriving when I'm forty.
With a house and **fifteen years** in, I could choose where I want to be.
do: Follow the same plan, less rushed: **solar, diploma, robotics**.
Invest steadily and maybe buy a **small rental flat**.
Look into **grid engineering** through a part-time degree.
feel: **Calm**, with a sense of having choices.
S4.quote: With ten years' notice, you can't say nobody told you.
fieldNote: Sara weighs a move into **grid engineering**, even though AI reaches it sooner.
She's driven by her **granddad's story** of a depot closing without warning.
A rental flat would add **a second income** alongside the line work.

steps.text: Study grid engineering through a part-time degree
Buy a small rental flat for extra income
Keep a steady monthly investment plan

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there isn't time to get good before the robots come. What would help is utilities running real robot trials now and putting experienced crews on them, instead of hiring outsiders who've never seen a pole.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether anyone asked the people on the ground. Every new system I've seen was designed by someone who never stood in a trench in the rain. If robots come, I want lineworkers in the room when they're designed.

headlineQuote: Every new system I've seen was designed by someone who never stood in a trench in the rain.
portrait: Sara is a 27-year-old **distribution lineworker** connecting new estates, solar panels and car chargers.
She **uses AI every day** and runs her crew's tablet.
She lives with Leo, a nurse, and invests monthly in **an index fund**.
She stays calm in most pictures and is **uneasy** only when robots come fast.
Her plan is to **run the robots**, through courses, trials and possibly grid engineering.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to get good before robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: Real **robot trials now**, with experienced crews put on them.
**Lineworkers in the room** when robots are designed.
